text: - ten metastasise to the skeleton and metastatic bone disease is a common problem with cancers of the breast, prostate, and lung. Bone metastases are often responsible for cancer pain (the general management of which is discussed on p.5) and also result in immobility, bone fractures, bone- marrow failure, spinal cord compression, and hypercalcae- mia.1 The most common sites of metastasis are the spine, hip, and femur. Primary bone malignancies are rare, and are usually sarcomas. Multiple myeloma (see Plasma Cell Neoplasms, p.658) also produces bone involvement. Management of bone metastases is essentially palliative since cure is rarely possible.1,2 External beam radiotherapy is the best treatment for localised metastatic bone pain, with responses occurring in over 70% of patients. Radia- tion delivered by bone seeking isotopes such as samarium- 153 or strontium-89 is an alternative.3-6 Bisphosphonates are of benefit in patients with severe bone pain that is too widespread for local use of radiotherapy and does not re- spond to other analgesics.2,7 Structural weakness due to extensive bone loss may re- quire structural support.1,2 Surgical fixation or stabilisation can treat or prevent fractures. Surgical excision and recon- struction with methylmethacrylate bone cement may also be required. Bone metastases cause local osteolysis and various inhibi- tors of bone resorption have been tried, not only to correct hypercalcaemia of malignancy (p.1083), but also to relieve bone pain and reduce the risk of fractures. Several ran- domised studies in patients with metastatic bone disease from breast cancer or multiple myeloma have shown 25 to 50% reductions in skeletal events with the use of the bis- phosphonates, clodronate or pamidronate.2,8 Similar re- sults have also been reported for zoledronate.9,10 Ibandro- nate is also used.11,12 A systematic review13 concluded that bisphosphonates significantly decrease skeletal morbidity, except for spinal cord compression. Various organisations have produced guidelines to suggest which patients are best treated with bisphosphonates.2,14,15 The clearest evi- dence is in patients who already have lytic destruction of bone. Treatment should start when bone metastases are di- agnosed and continue until no longer clinically relevant; they do not affect survival.13 Benefits in terms of skeletal events are only seen after about 6 months of treatment.12 There is much interest in the use of bisphosphonates to prevent the development of bone metastases. However, preliminary evidence of their efficacy is conflicting,16 and further large controlled studies are considered warrant- ed.2,15 Systemic antineoplastic therapy should also be given if the primary tumour is chemosensitive. Endocrine treatment is usually preferred for patients with breast and prostatic can- cers, and can produce useful control of symptoms from bone metastases.
